unit.title: Perform advanced welding using gas metal arc welding process GMAW -(Metal inert gas MIG)

summary: This Level 3 unit takes you beyond basic MIG welding. You will learn to work to a welding procedure specification (WPS); to choose and control short-circuit, spray and pulsed transfer; to set and calculate wire speed, voltage, inductance, stick-out, heat input, gas and wire use; to make multi-pass welds in all positions; to MIG weld stainless steel and aluminium; to control distortion; and to inspect, test, record and report while leading a team.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **advanced gas metal arc welding (GMAW)**: working to a WPS, choosing and controlling the metal transfer mode, choosing gas and wire, setting and calculating, multi-pass welding in all positions, MIG welding stainless steel and aluminium, controlling distortion, inspecting and testing, and leading a team.

A note on names: strictly, **MIG** (metal inert gas) means welding with an inert gas such as argon or helium, as used for aluminium. With gases containing carbon dioxide or oxygen, as used for steel, the process is also called **MAG** (metal active gas). In Jamaican workshops "MIG" is used for both, and so is GMAW.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and welders who lead MIG work on structural steel, frames, tanks, stainless food equipment and aluminium marine work.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Read a WPS and PQR, check welders are qualified, keep settings inside the ranges, and stop when a condition cannot be met.
Plan the joints, weld sequence, inspection points and resources; brief and supervise the team.
Set up and check the equipment
Set up the power source, wire feeder, gun and gas for steel, stainless steel and aluminium; find and fix feeding faults.
Choose and control the transfer mode
Choose short-circuit, spray or pulsed transfer for the job, and set wire speed, voltage, inductance and stick-out to get it.
Work out heat input, gas and wire use, fillet throat and leg sizes, and what a duty cycle allows.
Make multi-pass groove and fillet welds in the flat, horizontal, vertical and overhead positions (1G–4G, 1F–4F).
Change the set-up, gas, wire, cleaning and technique for these metals.
Plan tacking, sequence, presetting and weld size so the job stays in line.
Inspect before, during and after welding; know the common tests; find the cause of defects; record and report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on procedures, transfer modes, gases, wires, settings, calculations, positions, aluminium and stainless steel, distortion, defects, testing, safety, equipment and supervision.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example ER, PQR, pulsed spray, 3G, 4F, spool gun, fillet break test, backstep, backing strip, globular) and essays in full sentences, with calculations worked out.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: plan, weld and break-test fillet joints in the vertical-up (3F) and overhead (4F) positions to a WPS; and fabricate a square hollow-section frame with MIG, controlling distortion, and inspect it to the drawing.

blocks.note: Most questions at this level ask "which is best for this job, and why?" Learn each setting by its effect: what happens to the arc, the bead and the fusion when it goes up or down.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working to a WPS and leading the team

head: Document
What it is
rows: The written instructions for making a weld: process, base metal and thickness range, joint design, positions, filler class and size, gas and flow, transfer mode, polarity, wire speed or current and voltage ranges, travel speed or heat input, preheat and interpass temperature, technique and cleaning
The record of the test weld made and tested to prove that the WPS gives sound welds: the actual settings used and the test results
Proof that a welder has passed a test with that process, in the positions and thickness range it covers

ul: Each code lists **essential variables**: things such as the process, transfer mode, filler class, gas type, thickness range, position and preheat. A change outside the WPS limits on any of them needs a revised or new WPS, backed by a PQR.

Structural codes treat short-circuit MIG with care, because of its risk of lack of fusion on thicker plate. Under the AWS structural code, for example, a short-circuit MIG procedure must be qualified by test rather than taken as prequalified. Check what the code or procedure the Centre uses says.
A welder's qualification usually stays current only while the welder keeps using the process (often at least once every six months); otherwise a retest is needed.

flow: Read the drawing, the specification and the WPS; list the joints, weld sizes, positions and tests
Check that each welder is qualified for the process, positions and thicknesses
Check the materials against the drawing, and the wire class, size and batch and the gas against the WPS; make sure there is enough
Check every set: cables, gun, liner, contact tips, drive rolls, gas hose and flowmeter, return lead and clamp
Arrange screens, fume extraction, fire precautions and a clear, dry work area
Plan the weld sequence to control distortion, and mark the hold points: fit-up, after the root, after the cap
Brief the team: the WPS ranges, the sequence, the hold points and who does what; check they understand
Set up the weld record sheet before welding starts

ul: Watch that settings stay inside the WPS ranges. A welder working outside them "because it looks better" is stopped, the WPS is explained, and the welds already made are checked.
Never change the WPS to suit a welder's settings. A WPS can only be revised through the proper approval route, with a PQR where needed.
If a WPS condition cannot be met (the wrong wire in stock, no gas of the right mix), stop, tell your supervisor and wait for an approved answer.
Inspect before, during and after welding, not only at the end.

head: Job
Usual best choice
Why
rows: Long fillet welds on 10 mm steel frames
Thick plate fill passes in the flat position
Thin stainless food trays seen by the customer
Precise heat control and a clean finish
Root of a small stainless pipe with a purge
Wind blows away a MIG gas shield

sections.title: Equipment: set-up, checks and feeding faults

head: Part
What you need to know
rows: Constant-voltage (CV) DC, normally on **DCEP** (electrode positive) for solid wire. Inverter sets are light and often have synergic and pulse programs. Check the duty cycle on the rating plate.

Drive rolls push the wire: **V-groove** for steel and stainless, **U-groove** for soft aluminium, knurled for flux-cored. Roll pressure just enough to feed without slipping. A spool brake stops the spool over-running.

The **liner** guides the wire: steel spiral for steel; plastic (PTFE or nylon) for aluminium. The **contact tip** passes the current to the wire and must match the wire size. The nozzle and diffuser direct the gas. Keep the cable as straight as possible.
Cylinder chained upright; regulator and **flowmeter** (in litres per minute); hose and connections leak-free. CO₂ regulators can freeze at high flow unless a heater is fitted.
Fixed to clean metal on the job, close to the weld

blocks.p: **Duty cycle** is the share of a 10-minute period that a set can weld at a given current without overheating. A set rated 300 A at 60% can weld at 300 A for 6 minutes in every 10. At lower currents it can weld for longer. Duty cycles are measured at a set air temperature, so in a hot Jamaican shop a set reaches its limit sooner.

blocks.note: Most industrial MIG sets in Jamaica run on 220 V, 50 Hz. Read the rating plate, use a supply circuit that can carry the input current, and avoid long, thin extension leads: they drop the voltage and the arc becomes unstable.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Set the flow with a flowmeter; typical figures for steel are about 12–20 L/min (more for spray and large nozzles). Follow the WPS.
Too little gas lets air reach the pool: porosity. **Too much** is no better: the gas leaves the nozzle in a turbulent jet that pulls air in, and it wastes gas.
Even a light breeze (about 8 km/h) can blow the shield away. Use screens, and close doors upwind.
Spatter building up in the nozzle disturbs the gas flow: clean the nozzle regularly and use anti-spatter gel or spray on it.

head: What you see
Likely causes
What to do
rows: Contact tip worn, the wrong size or blocked with spatter
Roll pressure too low (slipping) or the wrong groove
Check liner, tip, rolls and brake in that order; blow out or replace the liner; straighten the cable
Wire blocked further on (tip or liner) while the rolls keep pushing
Soft aluminium wire in a long steel liner
Inlet and outlet guides out of line
Clear the blockage; fit the right liner, rolls and gun for the wire
Wire flattened by the rolls; fine metal dust in the liner
Reduce the pressure to the least that feeds without slipping; fit the right rolls; clean or replace the liner
Wire melts back and fuses to the tip (burnback)
Voltage too high for the wire speed (wire speed too low)
Tip held too close to the work
Balance voltage and wire speed; fix the feed; replace the tip
Wire stubs into the plate and pushes the gun back
Voltage too low for the wire speed (wire speed too high)
Raise the voltage or lower the wire speed, within the WPS
Tighten the brake just enough to stop over-run

head: Mode
How the metal crosses the arc
Typical conditions
Use
Watch out
rows: The wire touches the pool many times a second; each touch puts in a small drop
Low voltage (about 15–22 V) and current; CO₂ or argon-CO₂
Thin sheet, root runs, gaps, all positions
Low heat: on thick plate the weld can lie on the sidewall without melting it (cold lap)
Large, irregular drops, bigger than the wire, fall across the arc
Higher currents with CO₂ or low-argon mixes
Spatter and an irregular bead; flat and horizontal only
A fine stream of drops, smaller than the wire, crosses a steady arc without short circuits
Argon-rich gas (usually at least about 80% argon); current above the **transition current** (often about 200 A or more for 1.0–1.2 mm steel wire); about 24–32 V
Thick plate in the flat position and horizontal fillets (1G, 1F, 2F); high deposition, deep fusion, little spatter
A large, fluid pool: steel cannot be welded vertical or overhead with true spray; too hot for thin sheet; intense arc light
The set switches many times a second between a high peak current (one drop per pulse) and a low background current
Argon-rich gas; a pulse-capable (often synergic) set
Spray-type fusion with less average heat: all positions, thinner sections, stainless steel and aluminium
Needs a pulse set; settings come from its programs

blocks.note: 100% CO₂ cannot give true spray transfer. As the current rises, CO₂ gives globular transfer with heavy spatter. Spray needs an argon-rich mix.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: The settings and what they do

head: Setting
Effect
rows: On a CV set, the wire speed sets the **current**: more wire speed means more current, more deposit and more penetration.
Sets the **arc length**. Too low: the wire stubs and the bead is narrow and ropey. Too high: a long arc, a wide flat bead, spatter, undercut, and burnback.

Slows the rise of current when the wire shorts. More inductance gives a softer, wetter arc, a flatter bead and less spatter; too little gives a harsh, crackly arc and spatter; too much makes the arc sluggish and hard to start.

A longer stick-out heats the wire by resistance, so at the same wire speed the **current falls** and penetration drops, and the gas cover is further away. Often about 10–15 mm for short-circuit and 15–25 mm for spray. Keep it steady.
Too fast: narrow bead, undercut, poor fusion. Too slow: the pool rolls ahead of the arc, giving cold lap and lack of fusion, plus extra heat and distortion.

Work angle across the joint (about 45° for a fillet, 90° for a butt). Travel angle along it: a push angle (about 5–15°) gives a flatter bead, better view and better gas cover; a drag angle gives a narrower, more convex bead with deeper penetration.

blocks.p: A **synergic** set adjusts wire speed and voltage together from one knob, using programs for the wire and gas. It is still your job to check that the result is inside the WPS.
Heat input is the arc energy put into each millimetre of weld. **Heat input (kJ/mm) = (volts × amps × 60) ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000).**

ul: Raising the volts or the amps raises heat input; **travelling faster lowers it**, because the same energy is spread over a longer length.

**Too little** heat input can cause lack of fusion and a hard, brittle zone beside the weld that may crack. **Too much** causes distortion, coarse grain and lower toughness, and on stainless steel a loss of corrosion resistance.

If a test run is above the WPS limit, bring it down by travelling faster or lowering the settings within their ranges, then check again. Some standards also multiply by a process efficiency factor: use the method your WPS states.

head: Calculation
Method
Worked example
rows: 9 000 L ÷ 14 L/min ≈ 643 min, about 10¾ hours of arc time
1.0 mm steel wire weighs about 6.2 g per metre: at 10 m/min, 62 g/min, or about 3.7 kg an hour
300 A at 60%: 6 minutes of welding in every 10 at 300 A

head: Gas
Used for
Effect
rows: Deep, broad penetration; more spatter; no true spray; cheapest
Carbon steel, short-circuit and some pulsed work
Good all-round gas; less spatter than CO₂
Argon + about 5–10% CO₂, or argon + 1–5% O₂
Carbon steel, spray and pulsed transfer
Stable spray and a flat bead
Argon + about 2% CO₂ or 1–2% O₂, or a helium-argon-CO₂ "tri-mix"
The small active part steadies the arc; CO₂ is kept low so carbon is not added to the weld
Clean, stable arc with an oxide-cleaning action
Hotter arc: deeper, wider fusion and faster travel

blocks.note: Never use mixtures containing oxygen or CO₂ on aluminium: they oxidise the pool and spoil the weld.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Part of ER70S-6
Meaning
rows: Electrode, or Rod: the wire can be used as a MIG electrode or as a filler rod
Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal: 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa)
Solid wire (a T would mean tubular, flux-cored wire)
The chemical make-up: -6 has more manganese and silicon (deoxidisers) than -3, so it copes better with light mill scale or rust and wets out better. -3 suits clean steel.

blocks.p: The deoxidisers float to the surface as small, brown, glassy **silica islands**. Remove them between passes with a wire brush or chipping tool: left in, they can cause inclusions and lack of fusion, and paint will not stick to them.

head: Parent metal
Usual wire
Why
rows: L = low carbon, to reduce weld decay; Si = extra silicon for better wetting
Contains molybdenum to match 316's better resistance to salt and chemicals
Extra alloy allows for mixing with the carbon steel
Magnesium alloy: stronger, stiffer wire that feeds well; a close colour match after anodising
Silicon alloy: flows well and resists cracking; softer wire; turns dark grey when anodised

blocks.p: Always use the wire the WPS names. Store wire dry, in its packaging and off the floor; keep the spool covered in the feeder; use opened spools soon. Aluminium wire is the most sensitive: moisture and oxide on it cause porosity.
Pipe positions use 1G (rolled), 2G (axis vertical), 5G (axis horizontal, fixed) and 6G (axis at 45°, fixed).

head: Point
Vertical up
Vertical down
rows: Thicker plate and structural joints: the usual choice for 6 mm and over
Thin sheet, where burn-through is the main risk, and only if the WPS allows
Gun about square across the joint and pointing slightly upwards (about 5–15°); a slight weave or triangle with a pause at each side
Gun pointing slightly down; keep the arc on the leading edge of the pool, never letting the pool run ahead

ul: Keep the pool small: lower settings within the WPS, faster travel, stringer beads rather than wide weaves.
A short, steady stick-out and a slight push angle.
Spatter falls: leather jacket or sleeves, cap, gloves, closed collar; stand to one side of the arc, not under it.
Take the bevel angle, root face and root gap from the WPS, and check them before welding.

A **backing strip** is fitted behind a butt joint so the root can be fully penetrated without falling through. Tack it tight to both plates, with no gap underneath. The **root gap** lets the root run fuse both plate edges and the backing.
Ceramic backing tape gives a full-penetration root from one side and is removed afterwards.

flow: Check the fit-up against the WPS; clean the joint to bright metal
Tack: well fused, with tapered ends so the root can blend into them
Root run: fuse both edges (and the backing); watch the leading edge of the pool
Clean: brush or grind; remove silica islands; grind high spots and stop-starts
Fill passes: pause at each sidewall so it is fused, and avoid a wide, cold weave
Check the interpass temperature before each pass
Cap: just past the bevel edges (about 1–2 mm each side), with even reinforcement and no undercut
Inspect each pass before the next

ul: **Restarts:** grind the end of the stopped weld to a taper, start just before it and weld through, so the join is fused.
**Craters:** fill the crater before breaking the arc (use the set's crater-fill, or pause or step back briefly). An unfilled crater can crack.
**Interpass temperature:** check it with a temperature-indicating crayon or a contact thermometer. A crayon rated at the limit melts if the steel is hotter than its rating.

blocks.p: The weld and the metal beside it expand when hot and **shrink** as they cool, pulling the parts out of line (angular distortion, bowing, twisting).

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Weld only to the size on the drawing
Extra weld metal means extra shrinkage, wasted wire and time
Tack evenly; clamp or use a jig; check diagonals before welding
The parts start square and are held while the welds cool
Weld opposite sides in turn and work from the centre outwards, so the pulls cancel
Short runs welded against the overall direction, or spaced along the joint, spread the heat
Parts set slightly out of line the opposite way, so shrinkage pulls them straight
Measure squareness and diagonals as you go and correct early; record what worked

sections.title: MIG welding aluminium and stainless steel

head: Property
What it means for welding
rows: Conducts heat about three to four times as fast as steel
The start of a weld is cold: use the set's hot start or a higher start current (or preheat if the WPS allows), and expect to travel faster with more wire speed as the job warms up
Tough oxide film that melts at about 2 050 °C (the metal melts at about 660 °C)
Clean the oxide off just before welding; argon gives a cleaning action
Moisture, oil and dirty wire cause porosity
Does not change colour when hot
Treat every weld and part as hot; mark it
Expands about twice as much as steel
More distortion: tack closely and plan the sequence

head: Change from steel
Why
rows: Spool gun or push-pull gun (or a short, straight torch)
Soft aluminium wire bends and tangles in a long steel liner
U-groove rolls, light pressure, plastic liner
So the soft wire is not crushed or shaved
Contact tip made for aluminium, often one size larger
Hot aluminium wire expands and can seize in a tight tip
Active gases spoil the weld; helium adds heat
Aluminium wire to the WPS (ER4043 or ER5356)
Matched to the alloy, strength and finish
Gas cover and cleaning ahead of the pool; aluminium needs speed
Short-circuit gives poor fusion on aluminium

flow: Wash off any salt or dirt with clean fresh water and dry the parts
Degrease with a clean solvent and a clean cloth
Then brush the joint with a stainless steel brush kept only for aluminium (brushing before degreasing just spreads the oil)
Weld soon after cleaning: the oxide film starts to re-form at once, and dirt and moisture settle

blocks.note: Marina and boat work in Port Antonio, Ocho Rios, Montego Bay and the south coast is mostly aluminium and stainless steel. Salt spray and morning dew on parts stored near the sea cause porosity: wash, dry and clean them just before welding, and store wire in a dry cabinet.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Stainless steel conducts heat about a third as well as carbon steel and expands about half as much again, so heat stays in one place and **distortion** is greater.
Held at about 450–850 °C for too long, chromium next to the weld joins with carbon, and that zone can later rust (**weld decay**). Low-carbon (L) wires and low heat input reduce this.
Keep heat input low and respect the WPS **interpass temperature** (often about 150 °C). Pulsed MIG helps on thinner sections.

Use the stainless gas (argon with about 2% CO₂ or 1–2% O₂, or a tri-mix). The usual mild steel mix (for example argon with 20% CO₂) adds carbon and oxidises chromium, lowering corrosion resistance, and makes more spatter.
Use stainless-only brushes and grinding discs: iron from carbon steel tools leaves rust spots.
Remove heat tint after welding (stainless brush, polishing or pickling, as the job requires); back purge full-penetration roots where the inside surface matters.

head: Defect
Common MIG causes
Prevention
rows: No gas, too little or too much flow
Check gas flow at the nozzle; screens; clean nozzle; clean metal; correct stick-out
Pool rolling ahead of the arc (too slow, or too steep a drag)
Wide weave without pausing at the sidewalls
Settings to the WPS; keep the arc on the leading edge; pause at sidewalls; correct angles
Root gap too small or root face too big
Lower the voltage; steady speed; correct angle
Settings too high for the thickness
Lower settings; correct gap; vertical-down on thin sheet if allowed
Voltage and wire speed out of balance
Balance the settings; argon mix; add inductance; clean
Arc broken suddenly at the end of the run
A deep, narrow bead (deeper than it is wide)
Wider, flatter beads; lower current or slower travel; check the steel
Silica islands not removed between passes

head: Stage
What is checked
rows: Drawing, WPS and welder qualification; material and consumables; fit-up (angle, root face, gap, alignment); cleanliness; equipment
Settings within the WPS; gas flow; preheat and interpass temperature; each pass cleaned and inspected; sequence followed
Weld size (fillet gauge), profile, undercut, porosity, cracks, spatter; distortion and dimensions; NDT or destructive tests as specified

head: Test
What it shows
When it is used
rows: Surface faults, weld size and shape; it cannot see inside the weld
A fillet is broken over so its fracture face shows root fusion, porosity and inclusions
A cross-section, polished and etched, shows penetration, fusion lines, passes and leg sizes
A strip from a butt weld is bent round a former; lack of fusion and other flaws open up
Qualifying welders and procedures on butt welds (destructive)
Strength of the joint; hardness of the weld and HAZ
Cracks and pores that break the surface, on any metal
Cracks at or just below the surface of magnetic steels (not aluminium or austenitic stainless)
Flaws inside the weld: porosity, inclusions, lack of fusion, cracks
On the job, by qualified technicians (RT needs strict radiation safety)

ul: The code or specification says what is acceptable, for example the deepest undercut allowed. A defect outside the limits is recorded and repaired to an approved procedure: ground out completely, the removal checked, rewelded to the WPS, and inspected again.
Destructive tests are made on test pieces, never on the customer's job.

blocks.p: Each weld on a specified job is traceable: welder, WPS, wire batch, gas, settings, inspection and test results, repairs, dates. At the end of the job, the report to the supervisor gives: the job details and WPS; who welded what; consumables and settings used; inspection and test results, repairs and retests; time and materials against the plan; incidents and equipment faults; lessons for next time. It is clear, dated and signed.

sections.title: Health and safety for advanced MIG

head: Hazard
Why it matters
Controls
rows: Galvanised steel: zinc fume causes metal fume fever (a flu-like illness)
Stainless steel: fume contains hexavalent chromium and nickel compounds, which can cause cancer and lung damage
Remove coatings near the joint where the job allows
Local fume extraction close to the arc (hood or on-gun extraction)
A suitable respirator where extraction is not enough
Spray transfer, argon-rich gases and aluminium give very strong UV, which burns skin and eyes quickly and turns oxygen in the air into ozone, which irritates the lungs
Correct filter shade (darker for spray and higher currents; often 11–14)
Argon and CO₂ are heavier than air: they collect in pits, tanks and trenches and push out oxygen without any smell or warning
Permit, gas testing and forced ventilation
Never leave a gun or hose in a tank with the gas on
Falling cylinders, leaks, a frozen CO₂ regulator
Regulator heater for high CO₂ flow
Spatter, especially overhead; spray transfer makes parts very hot
Screens; combustibles cleared; extinguisher at hand
Full PPE; treat all parts as hot

blocks.note: Full welding PPE in Jamaica's heat is hard work. Drink water often, take short breaks out of the heat, and rotate heavy positional welding. Heat stress makes people careless.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the WPS, the PQR and welder qualification, and what an essential variable is.
I can plan a MIG job, brief the team and supervise the work to the WPS.
I can set up and check a MIG set, and find and fix feeding faults.
I can describe short-circuit, globular, spray and pulsed transfer, and choose the right one for a job.
I can explain the effect of wire speed, voltage, inductance, stick-out, travel speed and gun angle.
I can calculate heat input, gas and wire use, throat and leg sizes, and what a duty cycle allows.
I can choose the shielding gas and filler wire for carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium.
I can read a wire classification such as ER70S-6.
I can name the welding positions (1G–4G, 1F–4F) and choose vertical up or down.
I can make multi-pass welds with correct cleaning, restarts, crater filling and interpass control.
I can control distortion on a fabricated frame.
I can change a MIG set and my technique for aluminium and for stainless steel.
I can name the common MIG defects, their causes and their cures.
I can explain the main inspection methods and destructive tests, and when each is used.
I can keep weld records and write a job report.
I can control the fume, UV, ozone, gas and confined-space hazards of advanced MIG work.

terms: Backing strip
A strip fitted behind a butt joint so the root can be fully penetrated without falling through
Backstep welding
Short runs welded in the opposite direction to the overall progress of the weld, to control distortion
Burnback
The wire melting back and fusing to the contact tip
Cold lap
Weld metal lying on the plate or sidewall without fusing to it; a form of lack of fusion
Contact-tip-to-work distance
The distance from the contact tip to the work, which sets the stick-out
DCEP
Direct current, electrode positive: the usual polarity for solid-wire MIG
Duty cycle
The share of a 10-minute period a set can weld at a given current
ER70S-6
A solid steel wire: Electrode/Rod, 70 000 psi minimum tensile strength, Solid, with extra deoxidisers (6)
Essential variable
A WPS condition that cannot be changed beyond its limits without a new or revised, qualified procedure
Fillet break test
A destructive test in which a fillet weld is broken over to show its fusion
Globular transfer
Large, irregular drops, bigger than the wire, falling across the arc
Heat input
Arc energy per millimetre of weld: (V × A × 60) ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000), in kJ/mm
Inductance
A setting that slows the current rise during short circuits, softening the arc
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the joint just before the next pass is started
Macro-etch test
A polished, etched cross-section of a weld that shows its penetration and passes
PQR
Procedure qualification record: the record of the test weld that proves a WPS
Pulsed spray
Transfer in which the current switches between a peak and a low background many times a second
Short-circuit (dip) transfer
Transfer in which the wire touches the pool many times a second; low heat
Silica islands
Small glassy deposits from the wire's deoxidisers, removed between passes
Spool gun
A MIG gun carrying a small reel of wire, used to feed soft aluminium wire
Spray transfer
A fine stream of drops crossing a steady arc; needs argon-rich gas and high current
Synergic
A set that adjusts wire speed and voltage together from one control
Transition current
The current above which transfer changes to spray
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for making a weld

c1.title: Spray-transfer fill passes in Kingston
c1.text: Ackeem leads a team filling 16 mm single-V butt joints in the flat position (1G) at a structural shop in Kingston. The WPS calls for spray transfer with 1.2 mm ER70S-6 wire and argon with 8% CO₂, 26–30 V, 240–290 A, a travel speed of 300–450 mm/min, a maximum heat input of 1.6 kJ/mm and a maximum interpass temperature of 250 °C. The 1.2 mm wire weighs about 8.9 g per metre.

c2.title: Aluminium for a marina in Port Antonio
c2.text: Latoya leads the MIG welding of 6 mm 6061 aluminium handrails and gangway frames for a marina in Port Antonio, Portland. The finished parts will be anodised a silver colour. The parts are kept in an open shed near the sea, and in the mornings they are often damp with salty spray. The first 20 mm or so of each weld comes out narrow and humped, sitting on the surface without fusing.

c3.title: Practising for a 3G test in Montego Bay
c3.text: Tajay and two other trainees at a training centre in Montego Bay are practising for a 3G qualification test: 10 mm plate with a single-V preparation and a backing strip, welded vertical up with short-circuit MIG. One practice plate fails its bend test: a long flaw opens up along one side of the groove, where the weld metal lies against the bevel face without having melted into it.

c4.title: A stainless frame in St Ann's Bay
c4.text: Odane leads the MIG welding of a frame of 304 stainless steel square tube and 3 mm sheet for a juice processing line in St Ann's Bay, St Ann. The shop's usual gas is argon with 20% CO₂, used for mild steel. The WPS gives a maximum interpass temperature of 150 °C, and the work is in a corner of the shop with little air movement.

c5.title: Three problem stations in Old Harbour
c5.text: Kadeem is the team leader on a line making steel frames with short-circuit MIG at a shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine. At one station the wire keeps melting back and fusing to the contact tip at the end of a run. At another, the wire comes out of the drive rolls flattened, and fine steel dust is building up in the liner. A third welder's welds have started to show porosity, and his nozzle is half blocked with spatter.

questions.q: On a test run at 170 A, the arc crackles, keeps shorting and throws spatter, although the WPS asks for spray. What is wrong?
o: Too little current for spray: raise wire speed and volts
The gas is wrong: change to 100% CO₂ for a smoother spray arc
The arc is too long: lower the voltage to steady it
The stick-out is too short: lengthen it to about 35 mm
questions.why: Spray transfer starts only above the transition current, about 200 A or more for 1.2 mm steel wire. At 170 A the arc is short-circuiting; bring wire speed and voltage up into the WPS ranges.

questions.q: A pass is run at 28 V, 270 A and 300 mm/min. What is its heat input, and is it within the WPS?
o: About 2.5 kJ/mm: over the limit
About 1.5 kJ/mm: inside the limit
About 0.15 kJ/mm: well under it
About 15 kJ/mm: far over the limit
questions.why: Heat input = (28 × 270 × 60) ÷ (300 × 1000) = 453 600 ÷ 300 000 ≈ 1.51 kJ/mm, which is under the 1.6 kJ/mm limit. Travelling slower would push it over.

questions.q: At a wire speed of 9 m/min, about how much arc time will a 15 kg spool of the 1.2 mm wire give?
o: About 1 hour
About 28 hours
About 8 hours
About 3 hours
questions.why: 9 m/min × 8.9 g/m ≈ 80 g of wire a minute. 15 000 g ÷ 80 g ≈ 187 minutes, a little over 3 hours of arc time.

questions.q: After the second pass, small brown glassy spots sit on the bead surface. What should the welder do?
o: Weld straight over them, as the next pass melts them
Turn the gas flow up so the spots do not form
Remove them before the next pass is welded
Grind the whole pass away and weld it again
questions.why: These are silica islands from the wire's deoxidisers. Left under the next pass, they can cause inclusions and lack of fusion, so they are brushed or chipped off between passes.

questions.q: How can Ackeem check that a joint has cooled below the 250 °C interpass limit?
o: Spit on the joint and watch whether the spit boils
Judge it by whether the steel still glows dull red
Hold a hand near it to feel the heat coming off
Mark it with a 250 °C crayon: if it melts, wait
questions.why: A temperature-indicating crayon melts when the steel is above its rated temperature. A 250 °C crayon that melts means the joint is still too hot; a dry, chalky mark means it can be welded. Steel stops glowing well above 250 °C.

questions.q: Which filler wire suits these parts best, given that they will be anodised?
o: ER4043, which gives the best match once anodised
ER5356, which stays a close colour match
ER70S-6, as used for the steel frames
ER308LSi, which resists the sea air
questions.why: After anodising, welds made with 4043 (a silicon alloy) turn dark grey, while 5356 (a magnesium alloy) stays close to the colour of the 6061 parts. 5356 is also stronger and its stiffer wire feeds well.

questions.q: Why does the start of each weld come out narrow, humped and unfused?
o: Aluminium draws heat away fast; use the hot start
The argon flow is too high at the start of the weld
The wire speed is too high for the first 20 mm
The parts need a drag angle, not a push angle
questions.why: Aluminium conducts heat three to four times as fast as steel, so the cold plate takes the heat from the start of the weld. A hot start or higher start current (or preheat, if the WPS allows) gives fusion from the first millimetre.

questions.q: How should the damp, salty parts be prepared before welding?
o: Brush them with a steel brush, then weld at once
Weld them as they are, using a higher gas flow
Warm them with the torch until they are dry, then weld
Rinse in fresh water, dry, degrease, then brush
questions.why: Salt and moisture cause porosity in aluminium. Rinse off the salt, dry the parts, degrease, and then brush with the stainless brush kept for aluminium, just before welding.

questions.q: What fault does the opened-up flaw in the bend test show?
o: Porosity caused by too little shielding gas
Lack of fusion along the groove sidewall
Undercut at the toe of the cap pass
A crater crack at the end of the root
questions.why: Weld metal lying against the bevel face without melting into it is lack of sidewall fusion (cold lap). The bend opens it up. Pausing at each sidewall, keeping the arc on the leading edge of the pool and correct settings prevent it.

questions.q: How should Tajay hold the gun for the vertical-up passes?
o: Pointing about 30° downwards, to see the pool better
Pointing straight in, with a long stick-out
Tilted 45° towards one side of the groove
Square across the joint, tilted slightly upwards
questions.why: For vertical-up MIG the gun is held about square to the plate across the joint and pointed slightly up (about 5–15°), so the arc and gas reach both sidewalls evenly and the pool is supported.

questions.q: Why should Odane not use the shop's argon with 20% CO₂ on the stainless frame?
o: It adds carbon and oxidises chromium, so it rusts sooner
It is too cold a gas to melt the stainless steel properly
It gives spray transfer, which is too hot for 3 mm sheet
It makes the stainless steel turn magnetic as it cools
questions.why: High-CO₂ mixes add carbon to the weld and oxidise chromium, which lowers corrosion resistance and increases spatter. Stainless steel is welded with argon plus only about 2% CO₂ or 1–2% O₂, or a tri-mix.

questions.q: Which wire should be used for the 304 stainless frame?
o: ER316LSi
ER309LSi
ER308LSi
ER70S-6
questions.why: ER308LSi matches 304 stainless steel; the L (low carbon) reduces weld decay. ER316LSi is for 316, ER309LSi for joining stainless to carbon steel, and ER70S-6 is a carbon steel wire.

questions.q: What fume control does this job need in the still corner of the shop?
o: None, as MIG on thin sheet makes almost no fume at all
Extraction at the arc, and a respirator if needed
An open door at the far end of the shop is enough
A paper dust mask worn under the welding helmet
questions.why: Stainless steel fume contains hexavalent chromium and nickel compounds, which can cause cancer. With little air movement, local extraction close to the arc is needed, plus a suitable respirator where extraction is not enough.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the wire fusing to the contact tip at the end of each run?
o: Voltage too low for the wire speed
Gas flow too high for the nozzle size
Voltage too high for the wire speed
Return clamp fixed too near the joint
questions.why: When the voltage is too high for the wire speed, the arc climbs up the wire and melts it back to the tip (burnback). A hesitating feed or a wrong burnback-time setting can do the same.

questions.q: What should be done about the flattened wire and the dust in the liner?
o: Ease the roll pressure; clean or replace the liner
Fit a contact tip one size larger to pass the wire
Tighten the spool brake so the wire pulls straighter
Raise the wire speed so the rolls slip less on it
questions.why: Too much roll pressure (or the wrong groove) crushes and shaves the wire, and the shavings clog the liner. Set the pressure to the least that feeds without slipping, check the rolls, and clean or replace the liner.

questions.q: What should the third welder do first about his porosity?
o: Turn the gas flow up as high as the meter will go
Hold a longer stick-out so the nozzle stays cleaner
Clean the nozzle and check the flow at the nozzle
Change to a thicker wire so the arc is more stable
questions.why: Spatter in the nozzle disturbs the gas flow, so air reaches the pool. Clean the nozzle (with anti-spatter gel), then check the flow at the nozzle. Too high a flow causes turbulence, and a longer stick-out makes porosity more likely.

questions.q: A MIG repair is planned in the bottom of a deep machine pit. Why is the argon-CO₂ shielding gas a particular danger there?
o: It is lighter than air and gathers under the roof
It burns if a spark reaches a pocket of it
It turns into carbon monoxide when it is heated
It sinks and collects, pushing out the oxygen
questions.why: Argon and CO₂ are heavier than air, so leaked gas collects in pits and tanks and displaces oxygen, with no smell or warning. The work needs a permit, gas testing, forced ventilation and a standby person.

questions.q: A drawing calls for a fillet weld with a 5 mm throat. About what leg length must the welder aim for?
o: About 7 mm
About 5 mm
About 3.5 mm
About 10 mm
questions.why: For an equal-leg, flat-faced fillet, throat ≈ 0.7 × leg, so leg ≈ throat ÷ 0.7 = 5 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 7 mm. Measure it with a fillet gauge.

questions.q: A structural WPS specifies spray transfer for the fill passes. A welder wants to switch to short-circuit to make the job easier. What is the right answer?
o: Yes, as long as he keeps exactly the same wire and gas
Yes, if he slows down to make up for the heat
No: the WPS would need to cover that mode first
Yes, because transfer mode is a free choice
questions.why: Transfer mode is an essential variable: changing it needs a WPS that covers it, backed by a qualified procedure. Short-circuit on thick plate also risks lack of fusion.

questions.q: Which test finds cracks both at the surface and just below it on a carbon steel fillet weld, without damaging the job?
o: Dye penetrant testing (PT)
Magnetic particle testing (MT)
A macro-etch test on the weld
A fillet break test on the weld
questions.why: MT shows flaws at and just below the surface of magnetic steels. PT finds only flaws open to the surface, and macro-etch and break tests destroy the weld, so they are made on test pieces.
